short: The direct cost of the goods actually sold in a period.
seoTitle: Cost of Goods Sold — Meaning, Formula and Example
metaDescription: Cost of goods sold, or COGS, is the direct cost of the products actually sold during a period. The direct cost of the goods actually sold in a period.
definition: Cost of goods sold, or COGS, is the direct cost of the products actually sold during a period. It is derived from stock movement rather than from purchases, because buying stock is not the same as selling it.
bodyHtml:
Why Cost of Goods Sold matters

COGS drives gross profit and, in a kitchen or shop, is the largest controllable cost there is. Using purchases as a substitute makes every month with a big delivery look like a disaster and every month without one look brilliant.

Cost of Goods Sold formula

COGS = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock

Include freight and non-creditable taxes in purchases for an accurate figure.

How Cost of Goods Sold works in practice

Compute it from opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock, which means an actual stock count at period end. Restaurants often run this weekly on high-value categories such as meat and liquor rather than monthly on everything.

Worked example

₹80,000 opening stock, ₹4,20,000 purchases and ₹95,000 closing stock give a COGS of ₹4,05,000 for the month.

faq.question: Is COGS the same as purchases?
faq.answer: No. Purchases are what you bought; COGS is what you sold, adjusted for the change in stock.

faq.question: Does wastage go into COGS?
faq.answer: It ends up there through the stock count, which is why separately tracking wastage is the only way to see it.

formula.expression: COGS = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock
